title: TimeSAE: Causal Sparse Decoding for Time Series Explanations
one_liner: To explain what a black-box time series model actually uses to predict, extract the sparse features it needs and ground them in cause-and-effect tests.
lead: When a trained model predicts the next stock price or upcoming system failure, it is often a black box—you know what it says, but not why. Existing explanation methods work only for data patterns the model has seen before, and break when the data shifts. TimeSAE solves this by finding the smallest set of time-series features the model actually uses to predict, and checks them with real counterfactual tests to ensure the explanations are honest.

problem.h2: Why explanations fail on new data
paras: Today's time series models—trained to predict stock trends, equipment failures, or vital signs—are almost always black boxes. A model receives a sequence of numbers and outputs a prediction, but tells you nothing about which numbers in the sequence actually mattered. The naive approach is to ask: which past time steps did the model pay attention to? Or: if I erase a time step, does the prediction change? These methods work fine when you test them on data that looks exactly like the training data, but fall apart in the real world. The moment the data shifts—a different sensor, a new market regime, a seasonal pattern—these explanations become unreliable or outright wrong. The model is still predicting correctly, but the explanation for what it is doing has become dishonest.

The deeper problem is that an explanation must do two things at once: it must identify which features the model is using, AND it must prove those features actually cause the prediction (not just correlate with it). Existing methods skip the second part.

callout.html: Extract the minimal set of features a black-box time series model uses, and verify they truly cause the prediction by testing what happens when you change them.

steps.text: A sparse autoencoder (encoder and decoder pair) translates the time series into a small set of interpretable features—only a handful are active for each prediction.
The decoder reassembles these sparse features back into a time series that, when fed to the black-box model, yields the same prediction as the original data.
Change one feature at a time (e.g., flip a spike from positive to negative) and check: does the model's prediction flip too? If yes, that feature truly causes the prediction.
Train the encoder so it behaves like an inverse of the decoder, even on data it has never seen; this ensures explanations work on sensor shifts and new regimes.
Blend reconstruction accuracy, counterfactual faithfulness, and compositional consistency into one loss function and train end-to-end.

paras: The paper's move is simple: instead of asking the model directly which time steps mattered, build a learned sparse code (a small set of features) that the model responds to, and ground the explanation in counterfactual experiments—change the feature, watch the prediction, record causality.
object.object: sparse feature codes and their causal grounding

hidden.h2: Faithfulness: does the explanation truly explain?
hidden.name: Explanation faithfulness
paras: Faithfulness is a single concrete quantity: the fraction of times a feature is genuinely used by the black-box model to predict, as opposed to merely being correlated with the answer. If you change a feature and the prediction does not change, the feature is not faithful; it was a red herring. TimeSAE measures faithfulness by running counterfactual experiments during training: for each sparse feature, intervene (change it), pass the modified time series through the black-box model, and check whether the output prediction flips. A feature with high faithfulness will flip the prediction reliably when changed.

The paper estimates faithfulness using contrastive learning with counterfactuals. It generates alternative versions of the input time series by flipping key features, feeds them to the black-box model, and records which predictions change and which do not. This creates ground truth proof: a feature is faithful if intervening on it reliably changes the output, regardless of whether the feature is common or rare in the data.

heat.caption: Darker means higher faithfulness (feature truly causes prediction when changed). Marked features flipped the prediction in counterfactual tests.

reads.html: If you tweak a feature and the black-box model changes its prediction, that feature earned a high faithfulness score.
Faithfulness is formalized via counterfactual interventions: the model assigns high weight to features that produce contradictory label predictions when the features are changed.

mechanism.h2: Why causal grounding survives when data changes
paras: Standard explanation methods (like attention visualization) assume the model's logic is stable: if a time step mattered during training, it will matter when the sensor recalibrates or the market shifts. That assumption fails. The reason is that explanation methods learn a mapping from data patterns to explanations, and when the data looks different (new sensor, new season), that mapping breaks.

TimeSAE sidesteps this by extracting a sparse intermediate representation—a tiny code of important features—and grounding each feature in a counterfactual test: does changing this feature change the prediction? This test is agnostic to what the data looks like. It does not ask whether the feature is common or typical; it asks whether the model relies on it. Even if the raw time series looks different after a sensor shift, if the black-box model still uses the same sparse features to predict, the explanation stays valid. The method also enforces compositional consistency: the encoder is trained to be an approximate inverse of the decoder even on data the model has never seen, so explanations generalize.

stages.s: Decoder reconstructs using only those features
Counterfactual test: tweak each feature, rerun model
Measure: did prediction flip? If yes, feature is causal.
Minimal causal features + proof they matter

math.words: Total loss is a sum of four terms: reconstruction loss (sparse codes must decode well), label-fidelity loss (reconstruction must preserve the model's prediction), counterfactual loss (features must actually cause prediction changes), and compositional consistency loss (encoder inverts decoder on all data). All four are weighted and minimized together.
math.equation: L_TimeSAE = L_SAE + L_label_fidelity + alpha * L_cc + lambda * L_cf
symbols: Sparse autoencoder reconstruction loss; how well sparse codes rebuild the time series
Prediction preservation; how closely the reconstructed series yields the same model output as the original
Compositional consistency; how well encoder inverts decoder on unseen data
Counterfactual faithfulness; how often feature changes flip the black-box prediction
Weight on consistency (how hard to push generalization)
Weight on counterfactuals (how hard to enforce causal grounding)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a time series is 12 numbers: [9, 5, 2, 7, 1, 8, 3, 6, 4, 9, 2, 7].
Sparse encoder finds 3 active features: spike at position 4 (value 7), slow trend upward (0 to 9), and noise floor (all <3).
Decoder reconstructs: [8, 5, 2, 7, 1, 8, 3, 6, 4, 9, 2, 7] (close to original, only first value differs by 1).
Black-box model says original predicts failure=yes; reconstructed series also predicts failure=yes. L_label_fidelity ≈ 0 (good).

Counterfactual test: flip the spike at position 4 from 7 to 2. Reconstructed becomes [8, 5, 2, 2, 1, 8, 3, 6, 4, 9, 2, 7]. Model now predicts failure=no. This feature is causal, so L_cf reward is high.
Compositional consistency: encode-decode the reconstructed series again; get nearly identical result even though distribution may have shifted. L_cc ≈ 0 (good).
Final loss: 0.05 + 0.00 + 0.01 + 0.02 = 0.08 (low overall loss = good balance across all objectives).

math.note: The four terms together ensure the explanation is sparse, faithful to the model, causal (features truly matter), and generalizes beyond training data.

items.b: Extreme changes in the data still hurt.
items.html: If the new data is radically different from training (e.g., a different physical sensor or completely new measurement regime), the sparse features themselves may no longer apply, even if counterfactuals are valid. Causal grounding helps because it proves the features the model actually uses; but if the black-box model itself was only trained on one regime, it may not generalize, so the explanation stays honest about what the model learned, but the model is wrong.
Each feature requires a forward pass through the black-box model; with many sparse features or large models, the explanation cost can become slow.

items.b: Hyperparameters alpha and lambda must be tuned.
items.html: Balancing consistency, reconstruction, and counterfactual loss requires manual tuning or cross-validation; the wrong balance weakens explanations.
The extracted features are learned automatically and may not align with human intuition (e.g., a feature might be a mix of two physical quantities rather than one clean concept).
When all four losses are balanced and the sparse dictionary is large enough, explanations remain faithful even when the data looks different, and each feature has been proven causal by experiment.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic time series dataset with known causal structure: for instance, a fault detection system where failure happens if and only if the voltage spike exceeds a threshold AND the temperature ramp steepness exceeds a second threshold. Train a black-box neural network to predict failure from a longer noisy time series containing both. Then apply TimeSAE. The demo should extract exactly those two causal features (spike and ramp) from the noisy sequence, and the counterfactual test should confirm: flip the spike or ramp below threshold, and the model changes its prediction from failure to safe. Next, shift the data—add Gaussian noise, scale all values, or inject new sensor jitter—and re-run the counterfactual test. TimeSAE's explanations should remain stable, while a naive baseline method (e.g., visualizing which input numbers the model pays most attention to) breaks down.
demo.metric_eq: Explanation stability = faithfulness_on_original_distribution - faithfulness_on_shifted_distribution (lower is more stable)
demo.closing: The demo proves that TimeSAE's causal grounding stays valid when data shifts, while methods that only work on training data break down.
